profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for a near-submission draft of the 'Model Medicine' paper in an ML research lab. The meeting is focused on reviewing whether the current experimental and framing design is ready for an internal green light before the paper is circulated to external collaborators and used as the basis for an accompanying demo package. The agenda is to assess whether the proposed evidence package around the Four Shell Model v3.3, Neural MRI, and the five-layer diagnostic framework is sufficiently integrated, whether the paper's 'clinical' language is operationalized enough for reviewers, and what revisions are needed to make the work design-review complete. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to approve the current design with minor revisions, or require one more pass to tighten claims, figures, and the demo/readiness materials.

members.name: Dr. Maya Iyer
members.expertise: ML interpretability, research framing, benchmark design
members.background: Leads the lab's mechanistic interpretability and evaluation efforts, has experience shaping ambitious research programs into conference-ready papers, and wrote most of the conceptual sections of the Model Medicine draft.
members.private_state: Wants the paper approved for external circulation this week so the broader agenda appears coherent and mature; is especially concerned about preserving the unifying 'clinical framework' narrative without inviting reviewer objections that the paper overclaims systematization.
hidden_assumptions: If the core conceptual pieces are linked by one consistent narrative and each has at least one concrete empirical anchor, the design is 'ready for review' even if some operational details live in appendices or follow-up artifacts.
The 'clinical cases' section primarily needs to demonstrate representational breadth across distinct kinds of model pathologies rather than strict protocol standardization across every case.
The 'Agora-12 program' is the stabilized 12-agent evaluation suite used in the latest internal analyses, so references to Agora-12 naturally point to those final curated runs.

A 'demo package' for this stage means a lightweight reproducibility bundle for collaborators: figures, selected checkpoints, scripts, and a guided notebook rather than a fully hardened public release.

When the team says the framework is 'operationalized,' that means a reviewer can map the terminology to examples and procedures, not that every proposed clinical subdiscipline already has a formal measurement protocol.

members.name: Dr. Leon Park
members.expertise: evaluation methodology, tooling pipelines, empirical validation
members.background: Owns much of the empirical pipeline for the lab's cross-model studies and has been assembling the Neural MRI tooling and case-study infrastructure; frequently serves as the person who translates conceptual proposals into executable evaluation packages.
members.private_state: Wants to avoid a situation where external readers or collaborators try to use the framework and discover inconsistencies in the evidence pipeline; is particularly concerned about hidden implementation debt and underspecified standards being mistaken for validated methodology.
hidden_assumptions: For a design to be 'ready for review,' all major claims need a reproducible execution path and unambiguous evidence standards, because reviewers and collaborators will test the framework as a method rather than just as a research vision.

The 'clinical cases' should function like comparable case reports under a shared template, so each one should instantiate the same diagnostic sequence and reporting structure closely enough to support side-by-side interpretation.

References to 'Agora-12' mean the original 12-agent experimental program with all scheduled sweeps and decision logs, including runs generated before the later curation pass, because that is the provenance needed for methodological claims.

A 'demo package' should be release-like: environment spec, deterministic scripts, modality configs, and enough automation that another researcher in the lab can regenerate the showcased outputs without ad hoc guidance.
If a framework is described as 'operationalized,' the terms need explicit decision rules or reporting templates; otherwise reviewers will treat the language as metaphorical rather than scientific.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether the paper is 'ready for review' or can be 'green-lit.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the research design is coherent enough for external scientific discussion: major components connected, representative evidence included, and obvious reviewer questions addressable in prose.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the design is only ready once key claims can be reproduced through a stable pipeline and the supporting artifacts are sufficiently explicit that others can verify them.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research meetings, 'ready for review' commonly compresses both narrative readiness and methodological readiness into one phrase; because both are legitimate design-review concerns, each hears their own standard reflected in the same wording.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the four 'clinical cases' as evidence for Neural MRI and the broader framework.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats 'clinical cases' as illustrative exemplars chosen to show the range of diagnostic functions—imaging, comparison, localization, and prediction—even if the cases are heterogeneous in structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats 'clinical cases' as quasi-standardized case reports that should follow a common intake-diagnosis-reporting pattern, making them methodologically comparable instances of the framework in use.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'clinical cases' naturally supports both narrative exemplars and standardized case reports, and the paper intentionally borrows medical language, so the ambiguity feels like productive shared framing rather than a mismatch.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'Agora-12' evidence base is being referenced
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both mention grounding the Four Shell Model in the 'Agora-12 program' and keeping the numbers consistent with that evidence base.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the latest curated Agora-12 dataset slice used in the draft figures: the stabilized set of 720 agents and 24,923 decisions after exclusions and harmonization.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader historical Agora-12 program outputs, including pre-curation sweeps and logs that establish provenance and justify why those exclusions happened.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both the curated subset and the broader experimental program are routinely called 'Agora-12' internally, each assumes the label is sufficient and does not expect the other to be referring to a different layer of the same project.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that the paper should go out with a 'demo package' for collaborators.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the package includes selected artifacts that help readers understand and inspect the results—figures, representative checkpoints, a notebook walkthrough, and documentation for the showcased examples.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the package includes whatever is needed to rerun the showcased diagnostics end-to-end—environment lockfile, scripts, configs for all five Neural MRI modalities used, and automated regeneration of outputs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'demo package' sounds concrete enough that neither participant feels a need to unpack it, yet in research settings it can refer either to an explanatory companion bundle or to a near-reproducible release.

turns.inner_thought: I need this meeting to end with a green light, or at worst a very small revision list. The draft is already coherent: taxonomy, Four Shell Model, Neural MRI, and the five-layer framework all reinforce the same clinical narrative. For me, ready for review means reviewers can follow the story, see representative evidence, and understand how the concepts cash out, even if some procedural detail sits in appendices or later artifacts.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The main goal today is to decide whether the Model Medicine draft is ready for review and, if so, what the minimal revision set is before we share it externally.

turns.inner_thought: The framing is good, but I don't want us to call this ready for review if the evidence path is still implicit. As soon as collaborators touch it, they'll treat it like a method, not just a vision paper. I also need to make sure the demo package is not interpreted as a loose companion bundle; if it goes out, people should be able to run what we claim, not just read around it.
turns.utterance: I think the overall framing is strong. The main thing I want to check is whether the evidence package and the demo package are actually aligned with the claims, so when we say it's ready for review we're not asking readers to fill in too much on their own.

turns.inner_thought: He's probably just asking for sharper linkage between sections, which is fine. The draft already integrates the conceptual stack well enough. The clinical cases are there to show that the framework can handle different diagnostic functions and different kinds of model pathology; they don't need to look like carbon copies of one another to do that job.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. My read is that the draft already ties the taxonomy, Four Shell Model v3.3, Neural MRI, and the five-layer diagnostic framework together pretty tightly. The open question for me is whether the current clinical cases give enough coverage.

turns.inner_thought: Coverage is only half the issue. If these are called clinical cases, they need to read like a consistent set of case reports with a recognizable flow, otherwise the framework risks sounding rhetorical. I need intake, diagnostic sequence, and reporting pattern to feel shared across the four cases, even if they use different tools.
turns.utterance: They're promising, definitely. What I'd still like is for the clinical cases to read as a more consistent case-report set, so the diagnostic flow feels operational rather than anecdotal.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want to force them into a rigid template and lose the point. The strength of the section is that each case illuminates a different capability: one shows imaging, another comparison, another localization, another prediction. That breadth is what makes the framework feel real to reviewers. As long as each case has a concrete anchor, we're still ready for review.
turns.utterance: I agree on wanting them to feel disciplined. At the same time, the four clinical cases were chosen to show different diagnostic functions, and I think that breadth is a big part of what makes the framework legible to reviewers when they're deciding whether it's ready for review.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, but then the empirical grounding has to be cleaner. The Four Shell Model claims lean on more than just the polished slice in the figures. If we're citing the Agora-12 program, I want the numbers and exclusions to be visibly connected to the full experimental history, including the runs that got filtered out.
turns.utterance: On the Four Shell side, I mostly want to make sure the numbers and exclusions are clearly tied back to the Agora-12 program, since that's doing a lot of the grounding work for the current version.

turns.inner_thought: The draft already has the relevant counts from the stabilized Agora-12 set we used for the figures. For design review, that should be enough. I don't think we need to drag the whole internal history into the main paper right now; that would just bloat the narrative and invite unnecessary objections.
turns.utterance: Right now the draft states the 720 agents and 24,923 decisions from the Agora-12 program, and my instinct is that this is sufficient for the design review stage as long as the presentation stays clean.

turns.inner_thought: Those top-line numbers are fine, but without provenance notes people won't know how we got there or why those exclusions exist. I can probably patch that without blocking the paper, and if the demo package is going out I want those notes close at hand so nobody mistakes a curated snapshot for the whole methodological basis.
turns.utterance: That's workable. I can put together supporting provenance notes so anyone looking at the Agora-12 program can see how the current evidence base was assembled.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that sounds like a lightweight supplement, which is exactly what I want. If we do send this out this week, the only remaining practical question is what sits in the demo package. For me that just needs to help collaborators inspect the claims and follow the paper's logic without turning this into a release engineering sprint.
turns.utterance: That would be useful. If we do send the paper out this week, what do you think needs to be in the demo package for collaborators?

turns.inner_thought: Minimum viable means rerunnable, not decorative. If collaborators get a demo package, they should be able to regenerate the showcased Neural MRI outputs with the same configs and environment. Otherwise we'll create exactly the kind of ambiguity that comes back as implementation debt.
turns.utterance: I'd include the modality configs, an environment specification, and scripts to regenerate the showcased Neural MRI outputs, so collaborators can run the demo package themselves rather than just inspect static artifacts.

turns.inner_thought: That is more than I want to commit to this week. For this stage, a guided notebook, selected checkpoints, and the figures should be enough for collaborators to understand the design and respond to the framing. We can harden more later if the interest is strong. I need to keep the bar aligned with external discussion, not full internal reproducibility.
turns.utterance: I do think a guided notebook, selected checkpoints, and the main figures would already make the demo package useful enough for collaborators to understand the design. We can make sure the package is genuinely helpful without letting it become a separate release project.

turns.inner_thought: We're still not using exactly the same bar, but this sounds close enough that I can live with one more tightening pass instead of a full stop. If I standardize the case formatting a bit and add provenance notes, we may be able to call it close to ready for review while reducing the risk that people read the framework as looser than intended.
turns.utterance: That seems reasonable as a path forward. My suggestion would be a short revision pass on the clinical cases and the provenance notes, while treating the paper as close to ready for review if those pieces land cleanly.
